explanations.explanation: Genesis 39:1 says it plainly: Potiphar is an officer of Pharaoh, Egypt's king, and captain of the guard. So Joseph lands in the house of a man with real rank. I got bought for 25 cents, so a title like that makes me stand up a little straighter on my gold base.

Chief of the cupbearers is a title for a different kind of officer. Genesis 39:1 calls Potiphar captain of the guard. Plenty of titles float around a palace, friend, and it's easy to grab the wrong one.
I'll admit, chief of the bakers sounds like my kind of job. But Genesis 39:1 says Potiphar is captain of the guard. No mixing bowls in his title, friend, and no cookie boxes either.

“And the LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man…” (Genesis 39:2). Joseph is far from home and serving in a stranger's house, but he isn't alone. This is the heart of the whole chapter, so hold on to it.

Reuben is one of Joseph's brothers (Genesis 37:21), but this verse never puts him in Egypt with Joseph. Genesis 39:2 names who is with him: the LORD. That's company that doesn't have to catch a ride on a caravan.
The Ishmaelites are the traders who brought Joseph to Egypt, and verse 1 says Potiphar bought him from them. After that, they're out of the picture. Verse 2 says the one with Joseph is the LORD.

Potiphar noticed, friend. Verse 3 says, “When his master saw that the LORD was with him and made him prosper in all he did…” That's a man paying attention. Joseph's success wasn't happening in a corner.

Right, because the text says he saw it. Verse 3 reads, “When his master saw that the LORD was with him and made him prosper in all he did…” Potiphar saw both who was with Joseph and how things went for him. That's what leads to Joseph finding favor in his sight.
Verse 4 says, “Potiphar put him in charge of his household and entrusted him with everything he owned.” His household, friend. Joseph went from serving in the house to running it.
Potiphar is captain of the guard, so army feels like a natural guess. But verse 4 says he put Joseph in charge of his household. Joseph got the house and everything Potiphar owned, not the soldiers.

Granaries are storehouses, and the verse doesn't mention them. Verse 4 says Potiphar “put him in charge of his household and entrusted him with everything he owned.” It's the household. Remember that word.
“…the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s household on account of him” (Genesis 39:5). Blessing is the word the text uses. Potiphar's house got good things because Joseph was in it.
Warns is a fair thought, but it's not what the verse says. Genesis 39:5 says the LORD blessed the Egyptian's household on account of Joseph. No warning shows up here, just blessing.

Judges isn't the word here. Verse 5 says, “…the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s household on account of him.” Potiphar's household is on the receiving end of a blessing. That's good news for everybody under that roof.

The blessing doesn't stop at the field. Verse 5 says, “The LORD’s blessing was on everything he owned, both in his house and in his field.” Inside and outside, all of it. That's no small spill, friend.
That's it. Genesis 39:5 says, “The LORD’s blessing was on everything he owned, both in his house and in his field.” So it reaches the house and the field both. Nothing Potiphar owned was left out.

Verse 6 says Potiphar “did not concern himself with anything except the food he ate.” Joseph handled the whole operation and Potiphar kept the one job of eating. I can't judge him, friend. I've seen what happens when I lift the lid on a batch too soon.
Gold in a treasury sounds like exactly what a rich man would watch. But verse 6 says Potiphar “did not concern himself with anything except the food he ate.” Everything else he left in Joseph's care.

He's captain of the guard, so soldiers is a natural guess. But Genesis 39:6 says he “did not concern himself with anything except the food he ate.” Joseph had all he owned in his care, and Potiphar kept watch over his own plate.

Joseph says, “He has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife.” (Genesis 39:9). He lays out how much Potiphar trusts him, and then he says that one line is the exception. The whole answer rests on that.

A signet ring is a nice detail, but Joseph never mentions one here. In Genesis 39:9 he says Potiphar “has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife.” The one thing off limits is Potiphar's wife.
Joseph doesn't bring up a chariot, friend. In verse 9 he says, “He has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife.” That's the one thing Potiphar kept back.

That's right. Joseph tells her, “No one in this house is greater than I am.” (Genesis 39:9). He's pointing out how much Potiphar has trusted him with. And then he turns to the one thing he can't touch.
Joseph does say it. In Genesis 39:9 he tells Potiphar's wife, “No one in this house is greater than I am.” He's laying out how much his master has trusted him. Then he names the one thing held back.

explanations.answer: A great evil and a sin against God
explanations.explanation: Joseph asks, “So how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?” (Genesis 39:9). Notice he names God in his answer. It's a clear no, and he's looking at God when he says it.

explanations.answer: A great shame and a disgrace before Egypt
explanations.explanation: Joseph doesn't talk about Egypt's opinion here. His words in Genesis 39:9 are, “So how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?” He calls it evil, and he says it's a sin against God.

explanations.answer: A great folly and a dishonor to his father
explanations.explanation: His father doesn't come up in this answer, friend. In Genesis 39:9 Joseph says, “So how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?” God is who he names.
Verse 10 goes further than that. It says he “refused to go to bed with her or even be near her.” So he said no to the act and he stayed out of her reach too. This one goes beyond a single refusal.

Right, because the text says more than the no. Genesis 39:10 says he “refused to go to bed with her or even be near her.” She kept speaking to him day after day. He kept refusing, and he kept away from her.

explanations.answer: Leaves the cloak and runs outside
explanations.explanation: “But leaving his cloak in her hand, he escaped and ran outside.” (Genesis 39:12). He didn't stop to grab it. I've left things behind in a hurry, but never anything that mattered this much.

explanations.answer: Pulls free and calls for the servants
explanations.explanation: Verse 11 says not a single household servant was inside, so there was nobody to call. What the text says is that he left his cloak in her hand, escaped and ran outside (Genesis 39:12). He ran straight out of the house.

explanations.answer: Stays and tells her no once more
explanations.explanation: He had already said no, day after day (Genesis 39:10). This time verse 12 says, “But leaving his cloak in her hand, he escaped and ran outside.” He didn't stay to talk. He got out.

explanations.answer: That Joseph came to her and she screamed
explanations.explanation: She tells them, “He came to me so he could sleep with me, but I screamed as loud as I could.” (Genesis 39:14). That is what she says, and it isn't what verse 12 says happened. I think this is a hard part of the story, friend.

explanations.answer: That Joseph stole a cloak from Potiphar
explanations.explanation: A stolen cloak isn't what she says. In Genesis 39:14 she says Joseph “came to me so he could sleep with me, but I screamed as loud as I could.” The cloak comes up later in her telling, and not as something stolen.

explanations.answer: That Joseph ran away from his work
explanations.explanation: She doesn't call it running from work. Genesis 39:14 has her say, “He came to me so he could sleep with me, but I screamed as loud as I could.” It's a serious claim, and the text says it's not what happened.
She does mention it. Verse 15 has her say, “…he left his cloak beside me and ran out of the house.” The cloak shows up in her version, but it's her version.

The cloak is in her story. In Genesis 39:15 she says, “When he heard me scream for help, he left his cloak beside me and ran out of the house.” She tells the servants that part. Her whole account is built around it.
Verse 17 says, “Then she told him the same story…” So it's the same story she told the servants. She just tells it again to Potiphar.
That's it. Genesis 39:17 says, “Then she told him the same story…” She doesn't switch versions. Servants and husband both get the same account.
Verse 19 says, “…he burned with anger.” That's the word the text uses for Potiphar. It doesn't say who the anger is aimed at, so I'll leave that open too.
Shame isn't the word. Genesis 39:19 says Potiphar “burned with anger.” That's the feeling the text names.
Grief is a heavy word, but it's not the one here. Verse 19 says Potiphar “burned with anger.” Anger is what the text gives us.

explanations.answer: Has him thrown into the king's prison
explanations.explanation: Verse 20 says Potiphar “took him and had him thrown into the prison where the king’s prisoners were confined.” That is a hard turn for Joseph. I think this one hurts, friend.
Joseph was sold once already, so this guess makes sense. But Genesis 39:20 says Potiphar had him thrown into the prison where the king's prisoners were confined. No new master here.

explanations.answer: Sends him to work in the fields
explanations.explanation: The fields would be a step down, but they aren't the next step. Verse 20 says Potiphar had Joseph thrown into the prison where the king's prisoners were confined. It's a prison, not a field.

explanations.answer: He grants him favor with the warden
explanations.explanation: Verse 21 says the LORD “extended kindness to him, granting him favor in the eyes of the prison warden.” The LORD is still with him, even in a prison. It's the warden's eyes where the favor lands.

explanations.answer: He opens the prison doors at night
explanations.explanation: That would be dramatic, but it isn't in the text. Genesis 39:21 says the LORD “extended kindness to him, granting him favor in the eyes of the prison warden.” The kindness is favor with the warden.

explanations.answer: He makes Potiphar regret his anger
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about Potiphar's regret. Verse 21 says the LORD “extended kindness to him, granting him favor in the eyes of the prison warden.” The favor comes from the warden.

explanations.answer: Puts all the prisoners in his care
explanations.explanation: Verse 22 says, “And the warden put all the prisoners under Joseph’s care, so that he was responsible for all that was done in the prison.” All of them, friend. Joseph is behind those walls, and he's still given responsibility.

explanations.answer: Lets him walk out a free man
explanations.explanation: Not yet. Genesis 39:22 says the warden put all the prisoners under Joseph's care, which means Joseph is still inside. He's given charge of the prison, but he isn't freed from it.

explanations.answer: Sends him back to Potiphar's house
explanations.explanation: That's a neat guess, but the text doesn't say it. Verse 22 says the warden “put all the prisoners under Joseph’s care.” Joseph stays in the prison, and he's responsible for what happens there.

It's the other way around. Verse 23 says, “The warden did not concern himself with anything under Joseph’s care, because the LORD was with Joseph and gave him success in whatever he did.” The warden wasn't hovering. He left it to Joseph.

The warden is hands off. Genesis 39:23 says, “The warden did not concern himself with anything under Joseph’s care, because the LORD was with Joseph and gave him success in whatever he did.” Any boss would love to hand things off like that. The text gives the reason: the LORD was with Joseph.
